                                     PROJECT NO. 58481
 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                           §       PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION §                      §
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA §37.0561                     §                  OF TEXAS


                COMMENTS OF FREEPORT LNG DEVELOPMENT, L.P.

                                        I.   COMMENTS

       Freeport LNG Development, L.P. (“Freeport LNG”) submits these comments to address
new proposed §25.194(l) in the recent draft rule, which provides as follows:

       (l)     ERCOT operational standards.

               (1)    ERCOT may establish operational standards for large load customers to
                      ensure system reliability.

               (2)    A large load customer must comply with operational standards, developed
                      through ERCOT protocols, as a condition for interconnection and continued
                      operation of the customer' s load.

Freeport LNG is an LNG export company headquartered in Houston, Texas. The company’s
three-train, 17 MTPA natural gas liquefaction facility is the largest all-electric drive liquefied
natural gas (LNG) facility in the world, making it the most environmentally sustainable site of
its kind. The facility’s electric drive motors reduce carbon emissions by over 90% relative to gas
turbine-driven liquefaction facilities. Freeport LNG was formed in 2002 to develop, own and
operate an LNG terminal on Quintana Island, near Freeport, Texas. The terminal started LNG
import operations in June 2008 and began LNG export operations in 2019.

Freeport LNG’s operations indirectly support more than 30,000 jobs as a result of incremental
natural gas exploration, production, and processing associated with the LNG produced and
exported by its facilities. These LNG exports have a $5 to 7 billion net positive impact to the
U.S. economy each year. Locally, Freeport LNG is estimated to pay over $2.6 billion in taxes to
local taxing jurisdictions over its facility’s 20-year initial operating life

Since its founding in 2002, Freeport LNG has remained committed to corporate philanthropy and
being a steadfast supporter of the communities in which we operate. Freeport LNG is an integral
part of Brazoria County communities while employing over 350 full-time employees in Brazoria
County. Additionally, it is estimated that Freeport LNG’s activities contributed almost $640
million, directly and indirectly, to the Brazoria County economy in 2024 alone, as well as
supported almost 1,100 jobs in the county and provided $26.5 million in revenues for local taxing
jurisdictions in the same year.
                                                   1
 Freeport LNG is expressing concerns with the proposed §25.194(l) in the draft rule which subjects
new or expanded large manufacturing facilities to operational standards as pure retail customers.
Setting aside the legal question of whether ERCOT has authority over a pure retail load, we are
providing the following comments;

   -   Freeport LNG has been interconnected within the ERCOT region since 2008, and at no
       time during this period has ERCOT been given regulatory jurisdiction to assume control
       of our operations for system-reliability purposes. Freeport LNG coordinates directly with
       its utility regarding all operational, reliability, and power-quality matters. It is therefore
       unclear why a change to this long-standing framework is now deemed necessary.

   -   Freeport LNG does not participate in the ERCOT wholesale market. We rely on our retail
       electric provider to address service-related issues and to interface with ERCOT on our
       behalf. We do not possess, nor is it reasonable to expect us to acquire, the specialized
       expertise and resources required to monitor, interpret, and comply with a regional
       transmission organizations (“RTO”) operational standards.

   -   Large industrial facilities such as Freeport LNG already possess substantial inherent
       incentives to maintain and enhance their own reliability. Any reliability-related disruption
       results in unplanned downtime, lost production, and adverse financial impacts. These
       consequences create strong internal business drivers to pursue continuous reliability
       improvements without compromising equipment integrity, environmental compliance, or
       personnel safety. As a result, imposing additional operational standards on industrial
       facilities is unnecessary, as these entities are already motivated to avoid operational
       disturbances.

   -   Industrial facilities are not “one size fits all”. Different industries—and even different sites
       within the same company—operate with materially different processes, technologies, and
       equipment configurations, as well as operational constraints. ERCOT is not positioned to
       prescribe uniform operational requirements for entities that are neither utilities nor
       generators. Freeport LNG was designed and constructed in compliance with the applicable
       utility specifications at the time. We remain a customer of the utility—not of ERCOT–and
       continue to be in compliance with all utility specifications that were imposed upon it when
       the facility was interconnected to the utility.

   -   Any requirement that obligates our facilities to withstand grid conditions beyond our
       equipment design tolerances will present an unacceptable risk of substantial equipment
       damage, environmental non-compliance, and significant potential for injury or loss of life.
       Such risks cannot be assumed by Freeport LNG. ERCOT cannot be allowed to authorize
       or require operational standards that impose these risks on our facilities, our personnel and
       the general public.

   -   The prospect of undefined, evolving and/or unachievable operational standards applicable
       to existing industrial loads is of particular concern for a company that contributes
       substantially to state revenues and employs a large workforce. Subjecting existing
       industrial loads—particularly entities that are not engaged in the business of power
       generation or transmission—to potential disconnection for failure to comply with newly

                                                  2
     imposed ERCOT standards is unreasonable and threatens essential sectors of the state’s
    economy. New operational requirements could also prevent new development and the
    economic growth associated with such development if such operational requirements
    cannot safely be met by existing, proven technology.

-   If ERCOT and the Commission determine those traditional industrial facilities—such as
    oil, gas, LNG, and pipeline operations—cannot be categorically excluded from any
    operational-standards mandate, then all existing facilities should be fully grandfathered.
    Such grandfathering should remain intact notwithstanding any material modifications to,
    or expansions of, the existing facility, as the existing infrastructure (and its operational
    limitations) will remain fundamental to such modifications and expansions.

-   The system reliability concerns that have been most commonly expressed by ERCOT are
    from events that, in almost every instance, were caused by the applicable utility’s reliability
    and power quality issues—typically caused by a voltage magnitude excursion beyond the
    utility’s minimum threshold—that then had a knock-on effect to the operation of large
    industrial loads. As such, requiring changes to industrial load’s operational standards,
    rather than requiring utilities to increase their reliability of operations and the quality of the
    power they supply to those loads, is not a viable solution to the system reliability concerns.
    This is the proverbial situation of trying to have the tail wag the dog. ERCOT should focus
    on fixing the actual, underlying cause of system reliability concerns—which is the
    reliability and power quality of the utility—and not regulating retail customers.

-   Freeport LNG has communicated these concerns to ERCOT and the PUC on numerous
    prior occasions and strongly encourages ERCOT and the PUC to engage directly with large
    industrial stakeholders and the utilities to develop an alternative framework, rather than
    imposing operational standards that are ill-suited to industrial load operations and will not
    directly address the causes of system reliability concerns.


                                           Respectfully submitted,

                                           Freeport LNG Development, L.P.




                                           Senior Vice President, General Counsel & Secretary
                                           Freeport LNG Development, L.P.
                                           333 Clary Street, Suite 5050
                                           Houston, TX 77002
